prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: moving spoken dialogue agents beyond turn-based, half-duplex interaction toward genuinely synchronous, full-duplex behavior with overlaps, backchannels, and latency-aware turn-taking. The central idea is to adapt a pretrained autoregressive LLM into a wall-clock-synchronous dialogue model by interleaving two speaker streams in fixed-duration chunks, inserting periodic synchronization tokens, and training the model to predict both its own future speech and an estimate of the user’s near-future speech. The work is ambitious, timely, and clearly motivated by a real mismatch between current voice interfaces and human conversational dynamics. Overall, I found the paper interesting and potentially impactful, with a number of strong ideas, but also with several methodological and evaluation weaknesses that currently limit how convincing the empirical claims are.

The main strengths are conceptual clarity, practical relevance, and a plausible systems-level design. The paper identifies a real bottleneck in spoken dialogue modeling: standard LLMs lack an explicit notion of time, while full-duplex interaction requires synchronization to a shared clock and robustness to latency. The proposed chunked interleaving format with periodic speaker/synchronization tags is a neat way to inject coarse temporal structure into an autoregressive sequence model without changing the backbone architecture. I also think the latency-tolerant interaction mechanism is one of the more interesting contributions: predicting the missing current user chunk to enable generation of the next model chunk is a reasonable approximation to anticipatory processing in human dialogue, and it directly addresses deployment constraints such as network delay. The three-stage training recipe is also sensible from an engineering perspective, especially given the scarcity of dual-channel spoken dialogue data.

The paper’s strongest empirical message is that leveraging a text-pretrained LLM plus large-scale synthetic spoken dialogue appears to substantially improve semantic coherence relative to prior speech-only dialogue models such as dGSLM. The human evaluation results in Table 3 show a very large gain in meaningfulness over dGSLM while roughly preserving naturalness, and the out-of-distribution results on CANDOR are encouraging. If these findings hold under stronger evaluation, they would be significant. The interaction experiments between two SyncLLM instances trained on different datasets are also a nice demonstration that the framework is not tied to a single narrowly matched setting.

That said, my biggest concern is that the evaluation does not yet fully validate the paper’s central claim of “full-duplex dialogue agents.” Much of the evidence is in continuation mode, where the model generates both sides of the conversation from a prompt. This is useful for controlled analysis, but it is not the same as interactive full-duplex dialogue with a human or even with a realistic external user process. The interaction setting is simulated by coupling two instances of the same modeling framework with one-chunk latency. This is a reasonable first step, but it risks overstating the practical readiness of the approach. In particular, because both sides share the same tokenization assumptions, chunking scheme, and generative biases, the setup may be substantially easier than real user interaction with ASR noise, microphone variability, disfluencies, and unpredictable timing. The paper would be much stronger with even a small real-time interactive evaluation involving humans, or at least a more realistic pipeline where one side is external speech passed through the actual online tokenization and synchronization stack.

A second major concern is that the semantic evaluation is somewhat indirect and potentially fragile. The paper converts generated speech to text with ASR, discards overlaps, and then computes perplexity under a text dialogue model. This metric may correlate with semantic coherence, but it also conflates several factors: speech synthesis quality, ASR errors, overlap handling, and the biases of the reference text model. Since the paper’s key claim is improved meaningfulness, I would have liked to see stronger semantic evaluations: for example, transcript-based human judgments with overlap-aware instructions, response relevance or consistency metrics, or comparisons against text continuations conditioned on oracle transcripts. As presented, the perplexity analysis is suggestive but not definitive. The fact that overlapping speech is ignored in transcription is especially problematic for a paper whose main novelty is modeling overlap and synchrony.

Relatedly, the naturalness evaluation based on correlation of average turn-taking event durations with ground-truth continuations is interesting but limited. Correlation of IPU, pause, and FTO durations captures some timing statistics, but it does not directly measure whether generated overlaps occur in pragmatically appropriate places, whether backchannels are contextually sensible, or whether interruptions are cooperative versus disruptive. A model could match duration distributions while still producing unnatural conversational behavior. The human naturalness MOS partly addresses this, but the reported differences are small and mostly near parity across systems. In fact, the paper’s own results suggest that the main gain is semantic rather than interactional naturalness. That is still valuable, but then the title and framing around “full-duplex dialogue agents” should be interpreted more cautiously.

I also have concerns about the novelty relative to sequence-format engineering plus large-scale synthetic data. The paper presents synchronization tokens and chunk interleaving as the key mechanism for giving LLMs a sense of time. This is a clever representation choice, but the notion of discretizing time into periodic markers is fairly straightforward, and the paper does not deeply analyze why this particular design is optimal or necessary. For example, there is little ablation on alternative temporal encodings, chunk schedules, explicit duration tokens, or relative-time embeddings. Similarly, the deduplication/interpolation heuristic is practical, but under-justified. The interpolation step repeats deduplicated tokens uniformly within a chunk, which may distort prosody and timing in ways that are not captured by the current evaluations. The paper states that the effect is imperceptible up to 240 ms chunk size, but this is asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated.

The training pipeline raises additional questions. Stage 1 and Stage 2 rely heavily on synthetic speech generated from text dialogue using Bark with only 10 speaker presets. This is a huge amount of synthetic data, but its acoustic and conversational diversity may be limited, and synthetic turn-taking without overlaps may teach the model a somewhat artificial prior. The paper argues that Stage 3 with 2k hours of Fisher is sufficient to learn real turn-taking cues, but there is no ablation showing how much each stage contributes, whether Stage 2 is necessary, or how performance scales with the amount of real dialogue data. Since the paper’s practical contribution is precisely that 212k hours of synthetic data plus 2k hours of real data suffice, it is important to disentangle the value of architecture, representation, and training curriculum. At minimum, I would expect ablations removing Stage 1, Stage 2, deduplication, future-user prediction, and synthetic-data scale.

The comparison to baselines is another weak point. dGSLM is a reasonable historical baseline, but it is not obvious that it is the strongest available comparator for all aspects of this task, especially given the rapid progress in speech-text LLMs and spoken dialogue systems. The paper discusses SpeechGPT, USDM, SpiRit-LM, and others in related work, but does not compare against adapted versions of these models or against stronger cascaded systems. Since the paper’s main claim is not just semantic quality but full-duplex capability, a strong cascaded baseline with explicit turn-taking prediction, streaming ASR, text LLM, and TTS would be highly relevant. Even if such a baseline is imperfect, it would help clarify whether the gains come from synchronous joint modeling or simply from inheriting stronger text semantics from Llama3. As it stands, the comparison may be somewhat favorable because dGSLM is speech-only and older.

There are also some clarity and reproducibility issues. The paper is generally readable, but several implementation details are missing or too lightly specified for a top-tier conference standard. For example, I could not find enough detail on optimization hyperparameters, context lengths used in each stage, exact prompting/generation settings, how chunk boundaries are aligned with audio, how online tokenization latency is handled in practice, or how the vocoder is trained and conditioned. The interaction setup is especially underspecified: what exactly is the end-to-end latency budget, how much of it is model inference versus tokenization/vocoding/network delay, and are the reported 160–240 ms chunk sizes compatible with real-time deployment on the stated hardware? Since the paper emphasizes Internet-scale latency tolerance, actual runtime measurements would be very valuable.

The human evaluation is useful, but I would like more detail and stronger statistical reporting. Each item is rated by only three annotators, which is fairly light for nuanced judgments of dialogue meaningfulness and naturalness. The paper reports means and standard errors, but not significance tests between key pairs. Given that some differences in naturalness are small, significance matters. Also, because meaningfulness is judged from audio continuations relative to prompts, it would help to know whether annotators had access to transcripts, whether they could replay samples, and how overlap-heavy samples were handled. The MOS protocol is adapted from speech quality evaluation, but dialogue meaningfulness is a somewhat different construct.

A more conceptual concern is whether the model truly “runs synchronously with the real-world clock” in a substantive sense, or whether it simply conditions on periodic chunk markers that discretize time. This may sound semantic, but it matters for framing. The model does not appear to have continuous-time grounding or explicit latency calibration beyond chunked autoregression and future-user prediction. That is still a meaningful contribution, but the paper occasionally overstates the conceptual leap. I would encourage the authors to frame the method more precisely as chunk-synchronous autoregressive dialogue modeling rather than implying a broader temporal understanding.

Despite these criticisms, I do think the paper has real merit. The problem is important, the proposed representation is elegant, and the empirical results strongly suggest that text-pretrained LLMs can be adapted to spoken full-duplex dialogue more effectively than prior speech-only approaches. The work opens a promising direction at the intersection of spoken dialogue, multimodal LLMs, and real-time interaction. My overall assessment is positive but not unreserved: I see this as a strong idea paper with encouraging evidence, but one that still needs more rigorous validation and stronger baselines to fully support its headline claims.

The most important improvements I would recommend are the following. First, add ablations isolating the contributions of synchronization tokens, deduplication, future-user prediction, chunk size, and each training stage. Second, strengthen the interactive evaluation with either real human-agent conversations or a more realistic external-user simulation including ASR/tokenization noise and measured end-to-end latency. Third, broaden the baseline set, especially with a strong cascaded streaming system and, if feasible, a modern speech-text LLM adapted to the same setting. Fourth, improve semantic evaluation beyond ASR-plus-perplexity, ideally with transcript-based human judgments or overlap-aware relevance/coherence analysis. Fifth, provide more implementation and runtime details to support reproducibility and deployment claims.

In summary, this is an interesting and potentially impactful paper with a compelling problem formulation and a clever practical solution. The semantic gains over dGSLM are impressive, and the synchronization/chunking framework is novel enough to be worth attention. However, the current evaluation falls short of fully establishing that the system is a robust full-duplex dialogue agent in realistic settings, and the empirical story would benefit substantially from stronger baselines, ablations, and real interactive evidence. I would lean toward acceptance if the venue values forward-looking systems ideas and practical multimodal dialogue advances, but I also think the paper is close enough to the margin that these concerns are important.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper proposes SyncLLM, a method for converting a pretrained autoregressive text LLM (Llama3-8B) into a synchronous, full-duplex spoken dialogue agent. The core idea is to inject coarse timing via periodic speaker synchronization tokens and train the model on interleaved two-speaker HuBERT token streams, using deduplicated speech tokens to improve semantic efficiency. To address real-time latency, the model predicts an estimated current user chunk before generating its own next chunk, enabling operation under 160–240 ms chunking delays. Training proceeds in three stages: synthetic turn-based spoken dialogue from text, synthetic full-duplex dialogue without overlaps, and finetuning on ~2k hours of real dual-channel spoken dialogue. Empirically, the paper reports improved semantic quality over dGSLM via ASR-based perplexity and higher human-rated meaningfulness, while maintaining comparable naturalness and showing some robustness to out-of-distribution evaluation and simulated interaction between two SyncLLM agents.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: moving beyond turn-based spoken interfaces toward genuinely synchronous, full-duplex dialogue.
The proposed representation is conceptually simple and compatible with standard autoregressive LLMs, avoiding specialized dual-tower architectures and leveraging text pretraining.
The paper identifies a practical systems issue—network/input latency—and proposes a concrete anticipation-based mechanism for one-chunk delayed interaction.
The three-stage training recipe is pragmatic and makes effective use of abundant text dialogue data plus limited real spoken dialogue data.
Empirical results suggest substantial gains in dialogue meaningfulness over the main baseline dGSLM, including in human evaluation.
The paper evaluates both continuation and simulated interaction settings, which is more realistic than continuation-only evaluation.
OOD evaluation on CANDOR is a useful addition and suggests some degree of generalization beyond Fisher.
The work is clearly motivated by conversational science literature on turn-taking, overlaps, and backchannels.
weaknesses: The main empirical comparisons are narrow: the paper primarily compares against dGSLM, an older speech-only baseline, while omitting stronger modern cascaded or multimodal spoken dialogue baselines.
The claimed full-duplex capability is only demonstrated in simulation between two models, not with real human interactive experiments under actual latency and streaming constraints.
Several evaluation choices are indirect or weakly justified, especially ASR-transcribe-then-text-perplexity as a proxy for semantic quality in overlapping spoken dialogue.
The naturalness metric based on correlation of average event durations with ground truth is unusual and may not strongly measure conversational appropriateness or local timing quality.
The interpolation heuristic for reconstructing deduplicated tokens is ad hoc and may distort prosody/timing, yet is not rigorously analyzed beyond anecdotal claims of imperceptibility.
Human evaluation uses only 3 raters per item and relatively small sample sizes, with limited reporting of significance testing between key systems.
The paper does not provide enough ablations to isolate the contributions of synchronization tokens, deduplication, synthetic data stages, chunk size, and anticipation mechanism.
The method depends heavily on synthetic TTS-generated dialogue for pretraining, raising concerns about style mismatch and learned artifacts that are not deeply examined.
methodological_flaws: The semantic evaluation pipeline discards overlapping speech when converting generated audio to turn-based text, which is problematic because overlap/backchannel behavior is central to the paper's claimed contribution. This may systematically ignore errors or advantages specific to full-duplex dialogue.

Perplexity is computed with respect to a separate text dialogue model on ASR transcripts, but the paper does not validate that this metric correlates with human judgments of spoken dialogue meaning in this setting. ASR errors, overlap removal, and transcript normalization may confound conclusions.

The naturalness evaluation computes Pearson correlation between average turn-taking event durations in generations and ground-truth continuations given the same prompt. Matching corpus-level duration statistics is not equivalent to producing contextually appropriate turn-taking behavior; a model could achieve decent correlation while making locally unnatural decisions.

The latency-tolerance claim is only supported by simulated one-chunk-delayed model-model interaction, not by end-to-end deployment measurements with real streaming ASR/tokenization, inference, and vocoding latencies. Thus the claim of robustness to Internet-scale latencies is only partially substantiated.

The interpolation procedure assumes equal repetition of deduplicated tokens within a chunk when reconstructing periodic HuBERT sequences. This is a heuristic approximation with no quantitative analysis of reconstruction error, downstream vocoder impact, or sensitivity across chunk sizes.

The paper argues that periodic synchronization tokens give the model a sense of time, but there is no formal or empirical demonstration that the model learns temporal alignment beyond chunk indexing; this central mechanism lacks targeted ablation or probing.

Stage 2 constructs synthetic full-duplex data by pairing one speaker's speech with silence on the other channel. This does not expose the model to genuine overlap/backchannel phenomena, so the extent to which Stage 2 contributes to full-duplex behavior versus merely formatting is unclear.

Human evaluation reports means and bootstrap intervals, but the paper does not clearly report statistical significance for the key claim that SyncLLM maintains naturalness while improving meaningfulness, nor does it analyze inter-rater agreement.
